passage:
"Mumma, sit. SIT. I'll make your tea." Nandini put her hands on her hips.
"Nandini, you can't use the stove."
"Then I'll get the biscuits. You lie down. Don't cry today, okay?"
Shalini swallowed. "Beta, you don't have to look after me."
"Yes I do. Yesterday you cried and slept all day."
Nani came in from the balcony. "Nandini, come. Biscuits are my job. Your job is to play."
"But who will watch Mumma?"
"I will. I'm staying all this week, every day. And Mumma is seeing her doctor on Friday."
Nandini hesitated. "Every day?"
"Every day. You can check each morning."
Nandini climbed into Nani's lap.

qa.q: Who says she will be there every day this week?
qa.a: Nani says she is staying all week, every day.

qa.q: What might Nandini be worried about when she tells Mumma, "Don't cry today"?
qa.a: She may be worried that her mother will cry and sleep all day again, so she tries to take charge.

qa.q: What choice did Nani make, and why does it help Nandini?
qa.a: Nani took over the grown-up jobs and promised to be there every day, giving Nandini a steady adult so she can be a child again.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when her five-year-old tries to look after her?
qa.a: She may feel touched but also sad and worried, since she doesn't want her daughter carrying her.

grounding: A five-year-old bossily takes care of her struggling mother, and her grandmother steps in as a steady, consistent adult.

passage:
Class note, UKG-B, by Sharmila.
Payal, five, spent the morning managing everyone. "Ma'am, sit here. No, not there. Give me the chalk." At story time she clung to my sari, then hit my arm and ran to the corner. Ten minutes later she was back, stroking my hand. Her mother told me things at home have been very up and down lately.
What I did: kept my voice the same each time, kept the routine exactly as the chart shows, and said "I'm still here" after the hitting.
This afternoon I spoke to our school counsellor; we meet Payal's mother on Monday.

qa.q: What did Payal ask for at the start of the morning?
What might Payal be feeling when she clings, then hits, then strokes Sharmila's hand?
qa.a: She seems to need Sharmila badly but also feel unsafe about it, so she swings between holding on and pushing away.

qa.q: Which of Sharmila's choices helps Payal most, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the same calm voice and routine, and saying "I'm still here" after the hitting, shows Payal an adult who stays predictable.

qa.q: How might Payal's mother feel at Monday's meeting?
qa.a: She may feel anxious, but also supported, since the school is working with her rather than blaming Payal.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who bosses adults and swings between clinging and hitting, and responds with calm consistency and help from the counsellor.
